caption:
A developer used Claude to build Abyssal Garden, a swimmable underwater world that fits in one HTML file of about 97 KB.
No game engine, no images, no 3D models: every kelp leaf, fish and shipwreck is drawn by code when the page loads.
The developer says it runs at about 180 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti.

Would you play a game that an AI wrote from one prompt?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Wccftech · Photo: Noniv / GitHub
threads_text: Someone had Claude build a whole swimmable ocean, kelp forests, manta rays and a shipwreck, in one 97 KB file with no game engine and no images. It reportedly runs at 180 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti. Would you play a game an AI wrote from one prompt?

paragraphs.text: A developer has used Anthropic's Claude to build Abyssal Garden, an underwater world that visitors can swim through in a web browser and that fits in a single HTML file of about 97 KB. The project was posted to the ClaudeAI community on Reddit and covered by XDA Developers and Wccftech on November 15, 2026. Both outlets name the model as Claude Fable 5.2 in their headlines.

The project's own GitHub page describes a scene with towering kelp forests, light rays coming down through a rippling surface, a sunken wooden ship, a giant stone whale tail, manta rays, schools of fish and a purple grotto. The page lists the file at 96 KB and says it contains no images, no 3D models and no sound files.
How a whole scene fits in 97 KB

According to the repository, the seabed is sculpted on the graphics card each time the page opens and then decorated with about two million kelp leaves and plants, tens of thousands of rocks, and thousands of sponges, corals and fish. The ship, the whale tail and the animals are built from simple mathematical shapes, and the soundtrack is synthesized live with the Web Audio API.

The scene is drawn directly with WebGPU. Wccftech reports that the original prompt ruled out Three.js and Babylon.js, the two best known 3D libraries for the web, so Claude had to write the rendering code and shaders itself.

The prompt, which the developer published alongside the code, also set up a review loop. A separate AI agent was shown only rendered screenshots and a recording of a scripted fly-through, never the code, and was asked to list visual defects until none above minor remained. A second check measured GPU frame times during a 60 second flight through the scene.

The developer reports about 180 frames per second at 2560 by 1440 on an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, and the project page says a low end Samsung Galaxy A16 phone reaches about 20 frames per second on the lowest setting. Wccftech notes that these figures come from the developer and have not been independently verified.

Wccftech reports that the first version came from one detailed prompt and that later prompts added collision detection, a start menu and Low, Medium and High graphics settings. The work took about two to three hours of Claude processing, spread over roughly three days because of subscription usage limits.

The scene runs in Chrome or Edge on browsers that support WebGPU, with keyboard and mouse controls and experimental touch support. The code is published under the MIT license, so anyone can download the file, change it and rebuild it.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the size of the file is the striking part rather than the graphics alone. Procedural scenes that fit in tiny files have long been a showcase for expert programmers, and this one was produced by directing an AI model with a written specification and an automated reviewer. The approach of giving the model hard constraints and a separate critic that only sees the output is something other builders can copy.
Watch whether developers start shipping small browser games built this way, and whether independent testers confirm the reported frame rates on common hardware.
